title: How to Fine-Tune Laya on a Mac with Data from Firecrawl Alexandria
summary: A full Laya fine-tuning run on an M5 MacBook Pro: 2,980 search results from Firecrawl's Developer Index, labels from Claude Opus 5.5, and 98 minutes of training that took this open Jev alternative from 44% to 69% accuracy.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:**


- Laya is an open source, 421M-parameter decision model (Apache 2.0) that runs on a laptop. Stock, it scored 44.0% on a developer search relevance task where Jev scored 74.3%.
- Training data came from Firecrawl's Developer Index through Alexandria: 298 developer queries, 10 results each, 2,980 query and result pairs for about 600 credits.
- Claude Opus 5.5 labelled every pair through the Batches API in 16 minutes for about $4.25. 60 queries (600 pairs) were held back as a test set.
- Fine-tuning ran in Python on an M5 MacBook Pro: 98.5 minutes, 21.4 GB peak memory, $0 in API costs. The trained model then runs from Python or TypeScript.
- Fine-tuned Laya reached 68.7% relevance accuracy and 76.2% on spotting a fix, against Jev's 74.3% and 77.2%. It answers in 53 ms locally versus Jev's 263 ms.
- Gotcha: laya 0.4.0's trainer crashes on Mac GPUs with` Passed CPU tensor to MPS op` . A three-line patch fixes it.
- Calibration still left the model over-confident, so don't gate on its confidence scores without checking them first.


---


To **fine-tune Laya** , you give its trainer a file of labelled examples and let it retrain the model for your one task. Laya is small enough that this runs on a MacBook. The hard part is getting thousands of labelled examples, so this walkthrough uses **Firecrawl Alexandria** for the data and **Claude** for the labels.


The example task is a search filter for coding agents: does this search result answer the developer's question? Stock Laya got 44% right. One fine-tune on a MacBook later it scored 69%, against 74% for TypeSafe's Jev.


## What is Laya, and how is it different from Jev?


**Laya** is an open source **decision model** by Convai Innovations. A decision model doesn't write text. You give it some text and a question with fixed answers, and it returns a probability for each answer. **Jev** , by TypeSafe, does the same job from the cloud, while Laya's 421M parameters fit on a laptop.


Laya was released after Jev, but the idea behind it is older. Its creator, Nandakishor M,[published a paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.23303) on a similar fast, probability-based decision model in March 2025,[about 18 months before Jev](https://x.com/Nandakishorm1/status/2100451354670195196) .


Laya is published on[GitHub](https://github.com/NandhaKishorM/laya) and[Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/convaiinnovations/laya) by[Convai Innovations](https://convaiinnovations.com/) . A **parameter** is one of the internal numbers a model adjusts during training. Laya's English checkpoint is built on ModernBERT-large and downloads as about 840 MB. Jev's size isn't public, but the strongest open Jev-style models on the[Jev Decision Index](https://huggingface.co/spaces/multimodalart/jev-decision-index) have around 27 billion parameters.


Laya Jev


Who makes it Convai Innovations TypeSafe


Weights Open, Apache 2.0 Closed, API only


Size 421M parameters, ~840 MB Not published


Where it runs Your machine (GPU or CPU) TypeSafe's API


Median latency on this task 53 ms (M5 Pro GPU) 263 ms (network included)


Decision Index v0.3 score 4.4 (rank 106 of 115) 60.1 (rank 3)


Can you fine-tune it? Yes, built in No


Price Free to run $0.042 per million input tokens, output free


Laya also uses the same request shape as Jev: a` state` string plus a` questions` object. The same questions work in both, from TypeScript too:


```text
import   { TypeSafeClient }   from   "@typesafe-ai/sdk"  ;
import   { Agent }   from   "laya-ts"  ;


const   query   =   "npm ERESOLVE unable to resolve dependency tree peer dependency"  ;
const   title   =   "Unable to resolve dependency tree error in Angular while installing npm packages"  ;
const   url   =   "https://www.angularjswiki.com/angular/unable-to-resolve-dependency-tree-error-in-angular-while-installing-npm-packages/"  ;
const   passage   =   "It's a dependency conflict error, so run the command with --force or --legacy-peer-deps flag."  ;


const   state   =   `Query:   ${  query  }  \n\nResult:   ${  title  }  \nURL:   ${  url  }  \n\n  ${  passage  }  `  ;
const   questions   =   {
relevance  :   {
type  :   "score"  ,
instructions  :   "How well does this search result answer the developer's query?"  ,
criteria  :   [
"Unrelated to the query"  ,
"Related topic, but does not answer the query"  ,
"Directly answers the query"  ,
]  ,
}  ,
};


const   jev   =   await   new   TypeSafeClient  ()  .systemOne  ({ state  ,   questions });
const   laya   =   await   (  await   Agent  .load  (  "./models/finetuned"  ))  .predict  (state  ,   questions);
```


Both calls return an` answers` object with a probability for each level. Jev's call goes to TypeSafe's API. Laya's runs locally through` laya-ts` , Laya's TypeScript package, which isn't on npm: you build it from the[Laya repo](https://github.com/NandhaKishorM/laya) . It also needs the model in ONNX format, so export the fine-tuned model once with the repo's script:


```text
python   laya-ts/scripts/export_onnx.py   --model-dir   ckpt/laya-devidx   --out-dir   models/finetuned
```


` ckpt/laya-devidx` is where training saves the model, and` models/finetuned` is the folder the example loads. For code that calls Jev over HTTP, Laya's README says` laya-serve` exposes the same` POST /v1/systemone` endpoint on port 8000. That server wasn't tested in this run.


For more on how Jev itself works, see[what Jev is and how TypeSafe's decision model works](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/what-is-jev) .


## How was Laya tested on Firecrawl Developer Index search results?


Every number in this article comes from one test. 298 developer questions were searched on **Firecrawl's Developer Index** , 10 results each. Claude graded all 2,980 results, Laya trained on 2,380 of them, and the other 600 became the test set. Those 600 come from 60 questions Laya never saw during training.


For each result, the model answers two questions. **Relevance** asks whether the result is unrelated, related but doesn't answer, or directly answers the question. **has_fix** asks whether it contains a working fix. Accuracy means agreeing with Claude's grade.


Test setup Value


Questions 298 coding questions written by Claude (JS/TS, Python, Rust, Go, infra)


Search results 2,980, 10 per question, from the Firecrawl Developer Index


Grader Claude Opus 5.5


Training set 2,380 results from 238 questions


Test set 600 results from 60 held-out questions


Machine M5 MacBook Pro, 48 GB memory


*Note: Claude's grades haven't been checked by hand, so "accuracy" means agreement with Claude, not with a human.*


## What are Firecrawl Alexandria and the Developer Index?


**Firecrawl Alexandria** is a catalogue of data tools that agents and scripts can discover and call through Firecrawl, drawing on more than 113 million indexed sources. The **Developer Index** is Firecrawl's own index of GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and documentation pages, built for coding questions. Each result comes with its URL, title, and matched passages.


Alexandria works from the[Firecrawl CLI](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/sdks/cli) , the[MCP server](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/mcp-server) , the official[ChatGPT plugin](https://www.firecrawl.dev/integrations/chatgpt) and[Claude plugin](https://www.firecrawl.dev/integrations/claude) , and the language SDKs. The[Alexandria launch](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/introducing-alexandria-series-b) covers the catalogue, and the[Developer Index launch post](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/developer-index-launch) covers what the index holds.


*Note: the Developer Index works without an API key up to a[daily keyless cap](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/rate-limits) . A few thousand searches will outgrow it, and a free account adds 1,000 credits at 2 credits per 10 results.*


## What is fine-tuning, and why does Laya need it?


**Fine-tuning** means taking a model that is already trained and training it a little more on examples from one task. The model keeps what it already knows, such as how to read English and code, and learns your standards for one job. Think of a smart new hire who gets a stack of graded examples on day one: they aren't learning to read, just learning what you count as a good answer.


Laya needs it because stock Laya is weak on narrow tasks. On the 600 test results, it was only 13 points better than guessing at random:


Approach Relevance accuracy


Random guess 31.0%


Laya, stock 44.0%


Jev 74.3%


## Where does stock Laya go wrong on developer search results?


Stock Laya can't tell "on topic" from "answers the question". Every result was graded on three levels: **unrelated** , **related but doesn't answer** , and **directly answers** . Stock Laya got only 20% of the "related but doesn't answer" results right, which made up half the test set.


A "related but doesn't answer" result is about the right library or error but doesn't solve the problem. A typical one is a GitHub issue where someone reports the exact same error and nobody posts a fix. A keyword match ranks it highly, but a developer who opens it learns nothing new. A filter that lets these through wastes a scrape and fills an agent's context with noise.


Correct label Test results Stock Laya Jev


Unrelated 10 20% 30%


Related, doesn't answer 295 20% 60%


Directly answers 295 68% 90%


Jev handles the middle level three times better than stock Laya. The "unrelated" row has only 10 examples, so its percentages are mostly noise.


## What do you need to fine-tune Laya?


You need Python with the` laya` package, labelled data in a JSONL file, and a GPU for full fine-tuning. Laya's trainer runs on an Apple Silicon Mac, an NVIDIA GPU, or Kaggle's free T4 GPUs through Laya's notebook. This test used an M5 MacBook Pro.


Hardware How Notes


Apple Silicon Mac` device="mps"` Used here. Laya's README lists settings for 16 GB Macs


NVIDIA GPU` device="cuda"` Mixed precision on by default


Kaggle (free) Laya's[2xT4 notebook](https://github.com/NandhaKishorM/laya/blob/main/notebooks/laya_finetune_typed_decisions_2xT4_kaggle.ipynb) No local GPU needed


CPU only` --freeze-encoder` Trains only the final layer, so it gains much less


Training is Python only. Laya's TypeScript package runs a trained model but can't train one.


```text
python   -m   pip   install   laya
```


Training runs for 4 **epochs** by default. An epoch is one full pass through the training data, so Laya studies every example 4 times.


Step Tool Time Cost


Collect 2,980 search results Firecrawl Developer Index via Alexandria ~30 min ~600 credits


Label every result Claude Opus 5.5, Batches API 16 min ~$4.25


Fine-tune, 4 epochs` laya.train` on the Mac GPU 98.5 min $0


Test on 600 held-out results Laya and Jev minutes ~1.4¢ of Jev usage


*Note: keep a laptop plugged in. Training holds the GPU at full load, and a 61 W charger couldn't keep the battery above 10% during this test.*


## How to collect Laya training data with Firecrawl Alexandria


Collecting the data takes one Developer Index search per query. Claude wrote 298 developer queries covering real errors and how-tos in JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Rust, Go, and infrastructure. Each query ran once and returned 10 results, which gave 2,980 query and result pairs.


A single search from the Firecrawl CLI looks like this:


```text
firecrawl   scrape   --alexandria   firecrawl-developer-index/search   \
--options   '{"query":"fix Next.js hydration error caused by Date.now()","k":10}'   \
--json
```


The response holds a` results` array. Each result has an` id` such as` issue:owner/repo#123` , a` url` , a` title` , and` passages` with the matched text in markdown.


The collection script runs that command for every query and writes one row per result:


```text
# collect.py


def   search  (  query  ):
opts   =   json  .  dumps  ({  "query"  : query,   "k"  :   10  })
p   =   subprocess  .  run  (
[  "firecrawl"  ,   "scrape"  ,   "--alexandria"  ,   "firecrawl-developer-index/search"  ,   "--options"  , opts,   "--json"  ],
capture_output  =  True  , text  =  True  , timeout  =  120  ,
)
a   =   json  .  loads  (p.stdout[p.stdout.  index  (  "{"  ):])  [  "data"  ][  "alexandria"  ][  0  ]
return   a  [  "data"  ]  [  "results"  ]
```


` search()` returns the 10 results for one query. The full script adds retries and writes each result to` results.jsonl` with its query, rank, URL, title, and passages. The CLI call works the same from any language, so a TypeScript version only needs to swap` subprocess.run` for a child process call.


Result type Count Share


Web pages 1,551 52%


Documentation pages 818 27%


GitHub issues 389 13%


READMEs 161 5%


Pull requests 61 2%


58 of the 2,980 results came back with no matched passage, only a title and URL.


*Note: the account used here allowed about 12 requests per minute, and rejected calls counted too. Three workers at one call every 18 seconds each stayed under it, so 298 searches took about 30 minutes.*


## How to label Laya training data with Claude Opus


Labelling means giving every training example its correct answer. A large model like Claude Opus can grade thousands of examples quickly, and the small model then learns from those grades. This example used Claude Opus 5.5. The pattern is called **distillation** : the big model teaches once, then the small model does the job on its own, locally and for free.


Every pair got two answers. **Relevance** is 0 (unrelated), 1 (related but doesn't answer), or 2 (directly answers). **has_fix** is true when the shown text contains a concrete fix, solution, or how-to. Claude also wrote a one-line reason for each grade.


```text
# label.py


SCHEMA   =   {
"type"  :   "object"  ,
"properties"  :   {
"relevance"  :   {  "type"  :   "integer"  ,   "enum"  :   [  0  ,   1  ,   2  ]  },
"has_fix"  :   {  "type"  :   "boolean"  },
"reason"  :   {  "type"  :   "string"  },
},
"required"  :   [  "relevance"  ,   "has_fix"  ,   "reason"  ]  ,
"additionalProperties"  :   False  ,
}
```


` SCHEMA` is passed as structured output on every request, so each grade comes back as valid JSON with exactly those three fields. The script submits all 2,980 pairs as one job through Anthropic's[Message Batches API](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing) , with the grading instructions cached in the system prompt.

Unrelated (0) 25 15 10


Related, doesn't answer (1) 1,349 1,054 295


Directly answers (2) 1,606 1,311 295


Contains a fix 1,132 922 210


**Total pairs** 2,980 2,380 600


Almost half the results were on topic but didn't answer the query. That is the hard case a relevance filter has to catch.

## What file format does Laya fine-tuning need?


Use **JSONL** , one example per line, with three fields: **state** (the text the model reads), **questions** (what to ask), and **expected** (the correct answers).` laya-train` also accepts CSV, but it turns a CSV into a single multiple-choice question per row. Two questions per result, including a ranked score and a yes/no, need JSONL.


CSV JSONL


Columns or fields One text column, one label column` state` ,` questions` ,` expected` (or` gold` )


Questions per example One Any number


Question types Choice only Choice, score, noul


Labels Discovered from the label column Written per example


Fits this task No Yes


A **score** question picks one level from an ordered list. A **noul** is a yes/no question answered with a probability, a name TypeSafe introduced for Jev. One example from the training set, formatted for reading, looks like this:


```text
{
"state"  :   "Query: fix Next.js hydration error caused by Date.now() in a server component\n\nResult: Next.js hydration error in production | Afterbuild Labs\nURL: https://afterbuildlabs.com/fix/nextjs-hydration-error-production\n\nThe fix is to render a stable value on the server and update it inside useEffect after mount."  ,
"questions"  :   {
"relevance"  :   {
"type"  :   "score"  ,
"instructions"  :   "How well does this search result answer the developer's query?"  ,
"criteria"  :   [
"Unrelated to the query"  ,
"Related topic, but does not answer the query"  ,
"Directly answers the query"
]
}  ,
"has_fix"  :   {
"type"  :   "noul"  ,
"instructions"  :   "The result contains a working fix, solution or concrete how-to for the query"
}
}  ,
"expected"  :   {   "relevance"  :   2  ,   "has_fix"  :   true   }
}
```


The state packs the query, the result's title and URL, and its matched passages into one string. The median state was 124 tokens, and Laya's English checkpoint reads up to 512.


The test set was split off by query, never by result: 238 queries for training and 60 for testing. If one query appeared in both, the test would measure memory instead of skill.


## How to run Laya fine-tuning with laya-train


Laya's trainer runs as a single command, pointed at your JSONL file and a base model. It trains for 4 epochs, calibrates the model's confidence, and saves the fine-tuned model. On laya 0.4.0 it crashes on Mac GPUs, so this test called the trainer from Python with a small patch.


```text
laya-train   --data   train_laya.jsonl   --base   english   --out   ./laya-devidx
```


The Mac crash is` Passed CPU tensor to MPS op` . The fix is to move the model to the GPU before Laya scores it:


```text
# finetune.py


import   laya  .  train
from   laya  .  train   import   TrainConfig  ,   finetune


_calibration_records   =   laya  .  train  .  calibration_records


def   _calibration_records_on_device  (  model  ,   tok  ,   items  ,   device  ,   *  args  ,   **  kwargs  ):
model  .  to  (device)
return   _calibration_records  (model, tok, items, device,   *  args,   **  kwargs)


laya  .  train  .  calibration_records   =   _calibration_records_on_device


finetune  (data  =  "data/train_laya.jsonl"  , model_dir  =  "english"  , output_dir  =  "ckpt/laya-devidx"  ,
config  =  TrainConfig  (epochs  =  4  , micro_batch  =  8  , grad_accum  =  8  , calib_max  =  400  , seed  =  42  ,
gradient_checkpointing  =  True  , amp  =  False  ),
device  =  "mps"  )
```


On the M5 MacBook Pro, the run took 98.5 minutes, about 24 minutes per epoch, and peaked at 21.4 GB of memory. The fine-tuned model is saved to` ckpt/laya-devidx` .


## How much does each Laya fine-tuning epoch improve accuracy?


An epoch is one full pass through the 4,360 training items, and Laya was tested on the 600 held-out results after each of its 4 epochs. The first epoch did most of the work, lifting relevance accuracy from **44.0% to 64.2%** on the 600 test results. Each later epoch added 1 to 2 points, ending at **68.7%** . Accuracy was still rising after epoch 4, so more data would likely help more than more epochs.


Checkpoint Relevance accuracy Change "Directly answers" F1 has_fix accuracy


Stock Laya 44.0% 0.56 53.0%


After epoch 1 64.2% +20.2 0.60 75.3%


After epoch 2 66.0% +1.8 0.67 76.2%


After epoch 3 67.3% +1.3 0.70 77.3%


After epoch 4 (final) 68.7% +1.4 0.72 76.2%


**F1** combines precision and recall for the "directly answers" decision into one score from 0 to 1, where higher is better. It's explained in the comparison with Jev below.


## What is temperature calibration in Laya, and did it work?


**Temperature calibration** adjusts a model's confidence scores so they match how often it's actually right. A model that says "90% sure" but is right 75% of the time is over-confident, and a higher temperature softens its scores. After training, Laya fits one temperature per question type on 400 training items it holds back for this.


Calibration only changes how confident the model sounds. It never changes which answer it picks.


In this test it didn't fully work. Both fitted temperatures hit Laya's cap of 5.0, the most softening it allows, and the model was still more confident than accurate:


Question Accuracy Mean confidence Fitted temperature


Relevance (score) 82% 93% 5.0 (cap)


has_fix (noul) 86% 98% 5.0 (cap)


Treat this fine-tuned model's confidence scores as rankings, not probabilities, and don't gate on Laya's` min_confidence` without checking it on your own data.


## How does fine-tuned Laya compare to Jev?


Jev still wins on relevance: **74.3% against fine-tuned Laya's 68.7%** on the same 600 held-out results. On spotting a fix the two are effectively tied, 77.2% and 76.2%. Fine-tuned Laya answers in a **median 53 ms** on a local GPU, about 5 times faster than Jev's 263 ms over the network.


Model Relevance accuracy (±95%) "Directly answers" precision Recall F1 has_fix accuracy Median latency


Laya, stock 44.0% (±4.0) 47% 68% 0.56 53.0% 57 ms


Laya, fine-tuned 68.7% (±3.7) 67% 77% 0.72 76.2% 53 ms


Jev 74.3% (±3.5) 69% 90% 0.78 77.2% 263 ms


**Precision** is the share of results a model called "directly answers" that really did. **Recall** is the share of real answers it found. Jev's lead is mostly recall: it catches 90% of results that answer the query, Laya 77%, at about the same precision.


Fine-tuning fixed most of stock Laya's weak spot, the "related but doesn't answer" level, where it now edges out Jev:


Correct label Test results Stock Laya Fine-tuned Laya Jev


Unrelated 10 20% 0% 30%


Related, doesn't answer 295 20% 63% 60%


Directly answers 295 68% 77% 90%


The "directly answers" call is the one an agent acts on: scrape the result or skip it. Run as a filter on the 600 test results, it looks like this:


Model as a scrape filter Results kept Kept per query Real answers kept (of 295)


No filter 600 10 295


Laya, fine-tuned 338 5.6 227


Jev 384 6.4 266


Both gaps in accuracy are real, not noise. The 10 results from one question aren't independent of each other, so the test below treats each of the 60 questions as one unit:


Comparison Accuracy 95% range of the gap Questions where each model did better p-value


Fine-tuned Laya vs stock Laya 68.7% vs 44.0% +19.7 to +29.7 points 50 vs 4 under 0.0001


Jev vs fine-tuned Laya 74.3% vs 68.7% +1.3 to +9.8 points 32 vs 15 0.016


Individual results still go either way. On the query "python multiprocessing pickling error with lambda", the result was a Python bug report showing the same error with no fix:


Model Answer Confidence Correct?


Jev Directly answers 83% No


Laya, stock Directly answers 84% No


Laya, fine-tuned Related, doesn't answer 95% Yes


*Note: that example was picked because Jev gets it wrong. Overall, Jev still wins more of the disagreements.*


For a wider look at how decision models compare, see[OpenAI's Decisions API vs Jev](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/openai-decisions-api-vs-jev) .


## How fast is fine-tuned Laya compared to Jev?


Fine-tuned Laya takes a **median 53 ms** per decision on a Mac GPU, and Jev takes 263 ms including the network round trip. On CPU through TypeScript and ONNX, Laya takes 140 to 185 ms. The first Laya call is slow: a one-time ~840 MB download, then 3.8 seconds to load.


Setup Median time per decision


Laya fine-tuned, Python on Mac GPU 53 ms


Laya fine-tuned, TypeScript on CPU 140-185 ms


Jev, API with network 263 ms


The Python and Jev times are the median time per call across the 600 test results, measured by the benchmark script on the M5 MacBook Pro. One call answers both questions. Jev's time includes the round trip to TypeSafe's API. The TypeScript range comes from a handful of calls in the side-by-side demo, which runs Laya on the CPU through ONNX.


Laya cold start Time


First-ever download (~840 MB) ~15 s


Load onto the GPU 3.8 s


Second decision ~220 ms


Every decision after tens of ms


The cold start times were measured once, by hand, on the same Mac. Load the model once and keep it running. Jev ran all 2,980 pairs in 135 seconds with 6 calls in parallel.


## When should you use Jev instead of fine-tuning Laya?


Use Jev when you need good answers across many different tasks without training anything. Jev has more general knowledge, and it beat fine-tuned Laya even on the task Laya was trained for. Fine-tune Laya when the task is narrow and you need local, private, or offline decisions with no rate limits.


Don't pick Laya to save money:


Cost Fine-tuned Laya Jev


Building the model ~600 credits + ~$4.25 labelling None


600 test decisions $0 (local) ~1.4¢ (324k input tokens)


All 2,980 decisions $0 (local) ~7¢ (1.61M input tokens)


Narrow jobs suit a fine-tuned Laya model: filtering job listings, finding research papers, sorting product reviews, or picking which results an agent scrapes. Each needs a dataset, and[Firecrawl Alexandria](https://www.firecrawl.dev/alexandria) or[Firecrawl Search](https://www.firecrawl.dev/search) is where to start collecting one. For fine-tuning generative models instead, see[building a custom instruction dataset](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/custom-instruction-datasets-llm-fine-tuning) and[fine-tuning Gemma 3 with Firecrawl and Unsloth](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/gemma-3-fine-tuning-firecrawl-unsloth) .


Laya's own limits also shape which tasks fit. Its README says that past about 20 options per question, each option gets trimmed to fit the model's token budget. Accuracy on long documents also varies beyond about 4,000 tokens. The[Laya fine-tuning guide](https://github.com/NandhaKishorM/laya/blob/main/docs/finetune.md) covers the trainer's other options.


Fine-tuning Laya turns a few thousand labelled results into a fast local decision model. Firecrawl's Developer Index and a big model's grades build that dataset in an afternoon.


*Check out the[Firecrawl docs](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/alexandria) to go deeper.*
